issues.explanation: The profile is anchored to physical abuse by a romantic partner, but 'dark spaces' as a trigger and generalized threat from strangers are not well integrated with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise focus on the perpetrator and interpersonal/tactile reminders. This combination is possible, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking darkness to the abuse, darkness stands out as a poorly grounded trigger.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Feeling threatened by strangers in ordinary situations suggests broad generalized threat, but the rest of the profile does not provide corresponding appraisals or memory content to explain that generalization. The active formulation emphasizes Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, yet the selected strategies are mostly perpetrator- and social-contact-focused rather than stranger-focused, leaving this threat item insufficiently supported.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is an unusual target for avoidance in a case otherwise centered on partner abuse, tactile triggers, similar cars, and perpetrator reminders. It is not directly contradictory, but it does not cohere well with the other items or the active edge structure, because the threat content does not specifically concern familiar social contacts from before the event.

'Car Similarity' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is some clear motor-vehicle-specific trauma context, which is not otherwise represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The threat items are dominated by high immediate danger/re-experiencing states (flashbacks, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance), but the formulation has no active Triggers → Threat link and no Memory involvement; this makes a strong trigger-driven reliving/threat profile clinically incoherent with the specified network structure.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Avoidance of perpetrator reminders implies salient perpetrator-linked cueing, but the trigger set mixes direct offender cues with an idiosyncratic 'similar cars' cue that is not supported by the trauma type or by any memory/appraisal content explaining why vehicle similarity would be central.

vignette: Arthur Vance spent thirty-two years reading the sky for threats, but the violence that broke him lived in the quiet of his own kitchen. His late wife had been warm and charming until the whiskey bottles appeared, at which point her physical touch turned to bruises and her words to threats. He remembered the weight of her hands pinning his wrists, the sharp scent of alcohol clinging to her coat, the way her face would twist into a familiar, terrifying rictus. He had survived engine failures at twenty thousand feet, but domestic terror left him grounded in his own home, convinced that safety was a fiction he had never truly earned. Over the months that followed, ordinary sensations became inescapable. When a coordinator clapped him on the back at the regional aviation archive where he processed declassified squadron reports, the sudden physical touch sent his heart hammering against his ribs. He could not stay for the conversation. Seeing the offender-or even a man whose deliberate stride and heavy shoulders mirrored him-drove him to retreat behind rigid walls. The olfactory cue of spilled liquor at the coffee cart outside the reading room forced him to step back into the stairwell, pressing his palms flat against the concrete to steady himself. He learned to never allow himself to feel or express anger, instead steering clear of anything that reminded him of the person who had harmed him. He stopped attending squadron gatherings, telling colleagues he simply preferred the solitude of his archives work. The toll of living in constant alarm was relentless. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening to every creak of the house as if it were a warning shot. He remained superalert or watchful or on guard, scanning doorways and watching the way strangers held their glasses. Because his nervous system refused to power down, he avoided being emotionally close or intimate with others, convinced that any vulnerability would leave him exposed to the same helplessness he had endured. He managed the relentless tension by burying his feelings completely, treating his own body like a cockpit to be monitored rather than lived in. He would recount the evenings at the kitchen table with a flat, detached cadence that cut off abruptly when his voice tightened, refusing to let the past spill into his present. But this rigid containment only narrowed his world. By avoiding perpetrator cues and shutting down his emotional responses, he lost the chance to recalibrate his nervous system. He found that his avoidance of intimacy meant he lived in isolation, so when a former co-pilot finally called to discuss a restoration project, Arthur had to abruptly end the conversation, his trigger sensitivity now dialed to a painful maximum. The very strategies he used to survive kept him trapped in a state of perpetual reconnaissance, his avoidance of human contact ensuring that every residual sensory echo felt overwhelmingly dangerous. Suppressing his anger and isolating himself from contact did not quiet his body; it only starved it of the release it needed. The unexpressed frustration coiled tighter in his chest, manifesting as strong physical reactions when anything resembling the stressful experience surfaced. His shoulders stayed locked, his breath grew shallow, and his inability to allow himself to process the past meant his sleep vigilance worsened into chronic exhaustion. He would lie awake, superalert or watchful or on guard, until dawn, his body still braced for a blow that had long since passed. At seventy-four, Arthur Vance drives to a VA counseling center each Tuesday, not because he wants to, but because his grandson finally intervened after finding him collapsed at the hangar. He is most afraid of the quiet moments where his body betrays him, but he is hoping, however faintly, that someone might teach him how to rest without feeling like he is surrendering to the past.
